questions.stem: A 30-year-old male requires a blood transfusion after a severe car accident. He is known to have the Bombay phenotype. Prior to the transfusion, his blood sample is sent to the laboratory for compatibility testing. Based on his blood group, which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: Lack of H, A and B antigen on RBCs

options.label: B
options.text: Lack of H, A and B substance in saliva

options.label: C
options.text: Lack of antigens of several blood group systems

options.label: D
options.text: H, A and B antibody will always be present in se­rum

questions.answerText: Lack of antigens of several blood group systems
questions.solutionHtml:
>

Option A. His red blood cells lack H, A, and B antigens: This statement is correct. Individuals with the Bombay blood group do not express A, B, or H antigens on their red blood cells due to a homozygous mutation in the H gene (hh genotype).

Option B. His saliva does not contain H, A, and B substances: This statement is correct. The lack of H antigen also affects the presence of these antigens in body fluids, including saliva, because the H antigen is a precursor for A and B antigen synthesis.

Option D. His serum contains antibodies against H, A, and B antigens: This statement is correct. Because individuals with the Bombay phenotype do not express A, B, or H antigens on their red blood cells, they will form antibodies against these antigens if exposed.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Individuals with the Bombay phenotype lack A, B, and H antigens on their red blood cells and in their saliva, and their serum contains antibodies against these antigens.

In clinical transfusion practice the ABO blood groups are the most important and can never be ignored in red cell transfusion, because individuals, who genetically lack any antigen, have antibodies against the red cell types that they have not inher­ited. questions.answerText: Clumps of RBCs due to IgM mediated cold autoim­mune haemolytic anemia
questions.solutionHtml:
font-family:"Times New Roman",serif">Explanation:

Option B. Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA) involves IgG antibodies that react with red blood cells at body temperature, leading to their destruction by the spleen. This would not typically be associated with cold exposure and is not consistent with the symptom of cyanosis, which is related to cold.

Option C. Hemoglobinopathies, such as sickle cell disease, can cause hemolytic anemia, but the red blood cells do not clump in response to cold. Instead, hemoglobinopathies typically involve structural abnormalities of the hemoglobin molecule itself.

Option D. Cold agglutinin disease can sometimes involve IgG antibodies, but it is more commonly associated with IgM antibodies. IgG-mediated hemolysis at cold temperatures is much less common and would not explain the typical clumping seen in CAHA.

Educational Objective:

It is important to recognize the clinical and laboratory findings consistent with cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia (CAHA), where IgM antibodies bind to red blood cells at low temperatures, causing them to agglutinate. questions.stem: Hypochromic microcytic blood picture is least commonly seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.solutionHtml:
p>

Option A. Iron deficiency anemia classically presents with a hypochromic microcytic blood picture due to a deficiency in iron, leading to reduced hemoglobin synthesis and, consequently, smaller red blood cells with less hemoglobin.

 

Option B. Lead poisoning causes hypochromic microcytic anemia by interfering with several enzymatic steps in the heme synthesis pathway, leading to inadequate production of hemoglobin and microcytosis.

 

Option D. Sideroblastic anemia is characterized by the presence of ring sideroblasts in the bone marrow and can present with a hypochromic microcytic blood picture due to ineffective iron utilization and heme synthesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Rheumatoid arthritis is least likely to be associated with a hypochromic microcytic blood picture among the options provided, as it is more typically linked to normocytic or mildly microcytic anemia of chronic disease.

questions.stem: A 13-yr-girl with fatigue and weakness was found to be having reduced hemoglobin. Her MCV 70fl, MCH 22pg and RDW was 28. What is her most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Option B. Thalassemia minor often presents with microcytosis and a low MCH, but RDW is typically normal because the red blood cells are uniformly small.

 

Option C. Sideroblastic anemia can also present with microcytosis, but it is usually associated with ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow and may show elevated iron indices.

 

Option D. Thalassemia major presents with severe microcytic anemia, usually early in life, and patients are typically symptomatic with a history of blood transfusions.

 

Educational Objective:

 

An elevated RDW in the context of microcytic, hypochromic anemia is suggestive of iron deficiency anemia, which can be distinguished from thalassemia minor by the increased RDW.

Option C. Thalassemia minor often presents with microcytosis, but red cells are usually target cells rather than pencil cells, and other hematologic indices such as hemoglobin A2 levels can help in the diagnosis.

Iron deficiency anemia is characterized by microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells with the presence of pencil cells on the peripheral blood smear. questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

Option A. Total iron binding capacity (TIBC): TIBC increases in iron deficiency anemia. It represents the maximum amount of iron that can be bound to transferrin.

Option B. RBC protoporphyrin: RBC protoporphyrin increases in iron deficiency anemia. It reflects decreased availability of iron for heme synthesis.

Option D. Transferrin receptor: Transferrin receptor levels increase in iron deficiency anemia. It is a marker of increased demand for iron by erythroid precursors.

Educational Objective:

Transferrin saturation decreases in iron deficiency anemia, reflecting a reduced percentage of transferrin loaded with iron due to diminished iron stores, whereas total iron binding capacity, RBC protoporphyrin, and transferrin receptor levels increase in response to this condition.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old female presents with fatigue, weakness, and shortness of breath. Laboratory investigations reveal macrocytic anemia, and the FIGLU test is conducted to assess the etiology. FIGLU test is done for:
questions.solutionHtml:
:12pt">Explanation:

Option A. Vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to macrocytic anemia and is usually confirmed by low serum levels of B12 or elevated serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels, not typically with a FIGLU test.

Option C. Deficiency of thiamine leads to conditions like beriberi or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, not typically associated with macrocytic anemia or a positive FIGLU test.

Option D. Riboflavin deficiency is associated with symptoms such as angular stomatitis and glossitis, but not usually with macrocytic anemia, and it does not cause elevated FIGLU levels.

Educational Objective:

In patients with unexplained macrocytic anemia, a positive FIGLU test in the urine indicates a deficiency in folate. FIGLU is a biomarker for intracellular levels of folate.

questions.stem: Hypersegmented neutrophils are present in which of the following anemia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A. Hemolytic anemias are characterized by the premature destruction of red blood cells, but they do not typically cause hypersegmentation of neutrophils.

 

Option B. Iron deficiency anemia is characterized by microcytic and hypochromic red blood cells, and it does not usually result in hypersegmentation of neutrophils.

 

Option D. Aplastic anemia is characterized by a reduction in the number of all blood cell types (red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) due to bone marrow failure. It does not cause hypersegmentation of neutrophils.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hypersegmented neutrophils are indicative of megaloblastic anemia, a condition arising from impaired DNA synthesis which leads to abnormally large red blood cells and distinctive changes in neutrophils. This finding is not typical of hemolytic, iron deficiency, or aplastic anemias.

 

What are hypersegmented neutrophils?

 

Normal neutrophils have: 3–4 nuclear lobes.

 

Hypersegmented neutrophils: Diagnosed when:

Explanation:

 

Option A. G6PD deficiency is an intrinsic cause of hemolytic anemia due to a defect in the red blood cell enzyme G6PD, which is necessary to protect the cell from oxidative damage.

 

Option B. Hereditary spherocytosis is an intrinsic cause of hemolytic anemia characterized by a defect in the red blood cell membrane proteins that provide structural support, resulting in spherical red blood cells that are prone to destruction.

 

Option D. Pyruvate kinase deficiency is an intrinsic cause of hemolytic anemia due to a defect in the enzyme pyruvate kinase, which is involved in the glycolytic pathway of red blood cells, leading to a lack of ATP and subsequent cell death.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hypersplenism is an extracorpuscular cause of hemolytic anemia and not an intrinsic defect of the red blood cell itself, which distinguishes it from conditions such as G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, and pyruvate kinase deficiency that are intrinsic to the red cells.

 

Types of hemolytic anemia:

 

  • Intrinsic (intracorpuscular) defects → the problem is inside the RBC:
  • Membrane defects: hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis
  • Enzyme defects: G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency
  • Hemoglobinopathies: sickle cell, thalassemia

 

Extrinsic (extracorpuscular) defects → the RBC itself is normal; the problem is in the environment:

 

  • Autoimmune hemolysis
  • Mechanical trauma (prosthetic valves)
  • Hypersplenism
  • Infections, toxins

Educational Objective:

 

NESTROFT is a screening test for beta-thalassemia, which is based on the decreased osmotic fragility of red blood cells in this condition.

 

The NESTROFT test (Naked Eye Single Tube Red cell Osmotic Fragility Test) is a simple, cheap screening test used especially in countries like India to screen for β-thalassemia trait (carrier state).

 

How it works:

 

  • Based on the principle that RBCs in thalassemia are microcytic and hypochromic → they have a reduced osmotic fragility (more resistant to lysis in hypotonic saline).
  • In the test:
    • A single hypotonic saline solution (usually around 0.36% NaCl) is used.
    • After incubation, if the solution remains turbid → positive test (RBCs did not lyse → likely β-thalassemia trait).
    • If the solution becomes clear → negative test (RBCs lysed → normal).

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male presents with dark urine in the morning and has been found to have hemolytic anemia on laboratory evaluation. A diagnostic test reveals increased sensitivity of his red blood cells to lysis in acidified serum. Which of the following underlying defects is most consistent with these findings?

style="font-size:16px;">Explanation:

Explanation:

 

Option A. Thrombosis, particularly in unusual sites such as the hepatic or cerebral veins, is a well-recognized complication of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) due to the increased propensity for red blood cells to activate the complement system and the coagulation cascade.

Educational Objective:

 

PNH is characterized by hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, and thrombosis, but leukemia is not a feature of PNH but may be a secondary complication of the disease.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with history of recurrent infection and bleeding gums. On investigations the patient had pancytopenia and the peripheral smear showed macrocytes. The bone marrow biopsy showed no megakaryocytes and filled with fat globules. What is your diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
amily:"Calibri",sans-serif">Ans. B.  Aplastic anemia

Option B:

Explanation:

The given clinical presentation of a 12-year-old with recurrent infections, bleeding gums, pancytopenia, macrocytes on peripheral smear, absence of megakaryocytes in bone marrow, and the presence of fat globules in the bone marrow biopsy is suggestive of aplastic anemia. Aplastic anemia is characterized by a deficiency of all blood cell types (pancytopenia) due to bone marrow failure. The absence of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow biopsy indicates a lack of platelet precursors, which can lead to bleeding manifestations. The presence of fat globules suggests replacement of hematopoietic cells by adipose tissue in the bone marrow.

EXPLANATION:

Option A. Myelodysplastic syndromes :may also present with cytopenias and dysplastic changes in the bone marrow, but the absence of megakaryocytes and the presence of fat globules are not typical features.

Option C. ITP: is characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia without affecting other cell lines. It does not typically present with pancytopenia or the absence of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.

Option D. PNH:  is characterized by hemolysis, often presenting with hemoglobinuria. However, it is not typically associated with pancytopenia and fat globules in the bone marrow.

Educational Objective:

The clinical presentation of recurrent infections, bleeding gums, pancytopenia, macrocytes on peripheral smear, absence of megakaryocytes in bone marrow, and presence of fat globules in bone marrow biopsy is indicative of aplastic anemia. This diagnosis is supported by the bone marrow biopsy findings showing a lack of megakaryocytes, indicative of platelet precursor deficiency, and fat globules suggesting the replacement of hematopoietic cells by adipose tissue.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/458

questions.stem: Adult patient presents with generalized lymphadenop­athy and blood film shows 70% immature looking lym­phocytes. What should be the next best investigation?
questions.solutionHtml:
style="font-family:Aptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

Option A: Genotyping/Karyotyping is used to detect chromosomal abnormalities and gene mutations, which can provide information on prognosis and guide treatment, but it is not typically the first step following a blood film analysis showing immature lymphocytes.

Option C: Bone Marrow Aspiration/Biopsy is used to examine the morphology of marrow cells and architecture, which can confirm a diagnosis suggested by immunophenotyping, but it's usually not the first follow-up test when a specific leukemia subtype is suspected from a blood smear.

Option D: Peripheral Smear Study is an initial investigation that has already been performed, showing immature lymphocytes. This prompts further investigation with more specific tests like immunophenotyping, rather than repeating the same analysis.

Educational Objective:

The presence of immature lymphocytes in a patient with generalized lymphadenopathy strongly suggests a need for immunophenotyping to identify the specific type of leukemia. It may be chronic lymphocytic leukemia which can be picked up by certain surface markers like CD19, CD20, CD23, and CD5.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with pallor that required two blood transfusions previously. He has now developed fever and petechial haemorrhages. His hemoglobin is 9 g/dL, platelet count is 20,000/mm3 and TLC is 60,000/mm3. Flow cytometry reveals the cells to be CD10+ve, MPO+ ve, CD 19 + ve, CD 33 – ve, CD 117 + ve, and CD3 – ve. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
y:"Calibri",sans-serif">Explanation:

Option A: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL): ALL is a malignancy characterized by the overproduction of immature lymphoid cells, known as lymphoblasts, in the bone marrow. It is the most common type of cancer in children and is characterized by the presence of B or T lymphoid markers, but not typically myeloid markers. The flow cytometry results in the vignette showing CD10 and CD19 positivity suggest a lymphoid origin, which would be consistent with ALL. However, the presence of MPO, which is a myeloid marker, makes pure ALL less likely.

Option B: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML): AML is a malignancy of myeloid lineage cells and is associated with the presence of myeloid markers such as CD13, CD33, and myeloperoxidase (MPO). It usually presents with signs of bone marrow failure like anemia, infection, and bleeding due to dysfunctional hematopoiesis. CD117 can also be present in AML. In the given case, the presence of MPO and CD117 supports myeloid involvement, but the additional presence of B-cell markers (CD10, CD19) would be atypical for AML.

Option D: Undifferentiated Leukemia: Undifferentiated leukemia is a term used when leukemic cells do not express lineage-specific markers that allow classification as either myeloid or lymphoid. These cells may express non-lineage specific markers like CD34, HLA-DR, and TdT, but lack definitive markers for B-cell, T-cell, or myeloid cell lines. In the vignette, the presence of lineage-specific markers does not support the diagnosis of undifferentiated leukemia.

Educational objective:

  • B lymphoid markers: CD10, CD19 and CD79
  • T lineage markers: CD2, CD3 and CD7
  • Myeloid markers; CD13, CD33, CD117 and myeloperoxidase (MPO).
  • Non lineage specific markers of hematopoietic progenitor cells: CD34, HLA-DR and TdT

 

 

(Ref: Wintrobes 12th /1814-8, Dacie and Lewis hematol­ogy 10th /344-6)




Wintrobes 12th /1814-8, Dacie and Lewis hematol­ogy 10th /344-6)

questions.stem: Non-specific esterase is positive in all the categories of AML except:
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>erythroid precursors. It does not typically show NSE positivity because this enzyme marker is not associated with the erythroid lineage.

Explanation:

Option A: (M3 - Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia, APL): M3 or APL is characterized by a specific chromosomal translocation t(15;17), which leads to the production of the PML-RARA fusion protein. The morphological hallmark of APL is the presence of promyelocytes with heavy granulation and Auer rods. Nonspecific esterase staining may be positive in a minority of APL cases, but this is not the main diagnostic marker. APL is particularly associated with a risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and is treated uniquely with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide, which target the PML-RARA fusion protein.

Option B: (M4 - Acute Myelomonocytic Leukemia): M4 or acute myelomonocytic leukemia is characterized by the proliferation of both myeloid and monocyte cells. Nonspecific esterase staining is positive because of the monocytic component, distinguishing it from other forms of AML. These cells often show dual esterase staining when stained with both specific and nonspecific esterase, reflecting their mixed lineage.

Option C: (M5 - Acute Monocytic Leukemia): M5 or acute monocytic leukemia is characterized by an excess of monocytes in the bone marrow and blood. Nonspecific esterase staining is strongly positive in these cells, which reflects the presence of the monocytic component. M5 can be further subdivided into M5a and M5b, based on the maturity of the monocytes.

Educational Objective:

Non-specific esterase (NSE) staining is characteristic of M4 and M5 subtypes of AML due to their monocytic components and is not a feature of the M6 class, which is marked by a proliferation of erythroid precursors.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/618)

questions.answerText: Presence of testicular involvement at presentation
questions.solutionHtml:
u>

 

Option A: (TLC 4000-10000): Total leukocyte count (TLC) at presentation is an important prognostic factor in ALL. Normal or moderately elevated TLCs are generally associated with a better prognosis. A very high TLC, particularly above 100,000, is typically considered a poor prognostic indicator in ALL, particularly in T-cell ALL.

 

Option B: (Age between 1-10 years): age less than 1 year or more than 10 years has poor prognosis.

 

Option D: (Presence of blasts in peripheral smear): The presence of blasts in the peripheral blood smear is characteristic of ALL but on its own is not necessarily a poor prognostic indicator. The percentage and the total number of blasts can provide more specific prognostic information, with a higher burden sometimes indicating more aggressive disease.

The presence of testicular involvement at presentation in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is associated with a poorer prognosis due to the risk of extramedullary relapse and the need for more aggressive treatment.

  • CNS or testicular involvement

filtration and hepatosplenomegaly.

Explanation:

Option A: (M1 - Acute Myeloblastic Leukemia without maturation): M1 subtype is characterized by a proliferation of myeloblasts without significant differentiation. While organomegaly can occur, M1 is not typically associated with gum infiltration.

Option B: (M3 - Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia): M3 subtype is unique due to its association with the t(15;17) translocation and the PML-RARA fusion gene. It can present with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), but gum infiltration is less characteristic of M3.

Option C: (M2 - Acute Myeloblastic Leukemia with maturation): M2 subtype shows some degree of myeloid maturation. It can occasionally involve extramedullary sites, but gum infiltration and hepatosplenomegaly are more typical of AML with monocytic differentiation, such as M4 and M5.

Educational Objective:

Acute Myelomonocytic Leukemia (M4) is commonly associated with extramedullary manifestations such as gum infiltration and hepatosplenomegaly due to the infiltrative nature of the monocytic component of the leukemia.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 618)

Option A: (Acid Phosphatase): Acid phosphatase staining is primarily used to identify cells of the T-lymphoid lineage and is a key diagnostic marker in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It would not typically be positive in myeloid cells or AML.

questions.solutionHtml:
nic, leading to the development of APL.

Explanation:

Option B: t (9;22): This translocation is characteristic of Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML) and is known as the Philadelphia chromosome. It involves the fusion of the BCR (breakpoint cluster region) gene on chromosome 22 with the ABL1 (Abelson murine leukemia viral oncogene homolog 1) gene on chromosome 9, resulting in the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene. This fusion gene produces a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, contributing to the pathogenesis of CML.

Option C: t (17;21): This translocation is not a well-known chromosomal abnormality in leukemia. It doesn't correspond to a recognized leukemia subtype.

Option D: t (8;21): This translocation is characteristic of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) with maturation (AML-M2 subtype). It involves the fusion of the AML1 (also known as RUNX1) gene on chromosome 21 with the ETO (Eight-Twenty-One) gene on chromosome 8, resulting in the AML1-ETO fusion gene. This translocation is associated with a subtype of AML and is used in its classification.

The chromosomal translocation characteristic of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia is t(15;17), resulting in the PML-RARA fusion gene.

btype is generally associated with an excellent prognosis.

Excisional biopsy reveals a nodular pattern with a predominance of lymphocytes, and characteristic large, atypical mononuclear or multinucleated cells with a "popcorn" appearance. Immunohistochemistry shows positive staining for CD20 and CD45. What subtype of Hodgkin's lymphoma is most likely to be diagnosed in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
>

Option A:

 

 

Explanation:

 

Option B: (Lymphocyte depleted Hodgkin's lymphoma): This rare subtype is marked by a lack of lymphocytes and an abundance of classic Reed-Sternberg cells. It often presents in more advanced stages and has a worse prognosis. It does not typically contain popcorn cells.

 

Option C: (Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin's lymphoma): The most common subtype, characterized by the presence of collagen bands dividing the lymph node into nodules and Reed-Sternberg cells within lacunar spaces. This subtype usually affects young adults, and it is not primarily associated with popcorn cells.

Educational Objective:

 

A biopsy showing a nodular pattern with a predominance of lymphocytes and characteristic "popcorn" cells that are positive for CD20 and CD45 is diagnostic of Lymphocyte Predominant Hodgkin's Lymphoma.

ily:Aptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

,sans-serif">Option A: Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML) is characterized by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome and an increase in myeloid cells, particularly granulocytes. Smudge cells are not a typical feature of CML.

Smudge cells in the peripheral smear are characteristic of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL), due to the increased fragility of the abnormal lymphocytes encountered in this disease.

questions.solutionHtml:
ze:12pt">Explanation:

Option A: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML): is characterized by the rapid growth of abnormal myeloid cells in the bone marrow. While AML may show increased myeloid cells in the peripheral smear, it typically presents with blasts and a decrease in mature cells, unlike the broad spectrum of increased cells seen in the question.

Option B: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL): primarily affects lymphoid cells. It is characterized by the presence of lymphoblasts in the peripheral blood. The question describes an increase in myeloid cell lineages (neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils, and platelets), making ALL less likely.

Option D: Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS): is a group of disorders characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis. While MDS can present with cytopenias and dysplastic changes in blood cells, the specific pattern described in the question (increased neutrophils, basophils, eosinophils, and platelets) is more indicative of CML.

Chronic myeloid leukemia is a stem cell disease that is characterized by leukocytosis with granulocytic immaturities, basophilia, splenomegaly and distinct chromosomal abnormality Philadelphia chromosome.

His peripheral smear shows metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophilia and basophilia (image given for reference). Which of the following is the likely genetic anomaly present in this individual?

t-family:Aptos,sans-serif">The dragging sensation (can be due to splenomegaly seen in CML patients)

Explanation:

Option B: t (15;17): is associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). It involves the fusion of the PML (promyelocytic leukemia) gene on chromosome 15 with the RARA (retinoic acid receptor alpha) gene on chromosome 17, resulting in the PML-RARA fusion gene. This fusion gene plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of APL.

Option C: t (8;14): is associated with Burkitt's lymphoma. It involves the c-MYC gene on chromosome 8 and the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene on chromosome 14. The dysregulation of c-MYC, a proto-oncogene, contributes to the rapid and uncontrolled proliferation of B cells in Burkitt's lymphoma.

Option D: t (8;21): is associated with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), particularly the subtype known as AML with t(8;21), also called AML-M2. It involves the fusion of the AML1 (acute myeloid leukemia 1) gene on chromosome 21 with the ETO (eight-twenty-one) gene on chromosome 8, resulting in the AML1-ETO fusion gene.

Educational Objective:

The genetic anomaly likely present in an elderly male with an elevated leukocyte and platelet count, peripheral smear showing metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophilia, and basophilia is t (9;22), which is associated with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male presents with fatigue and widespread purpura. Blood work reveals a marked decrease in platelets, with counts persistently below 20,000/µL. The patient's history includes recurrent epistaxis and one instance of hematuria. Bone marrow biopsy reveals a hypocellular marrow with a markedly reduced number of megakaryocytes. All of the following can cause megakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, except:
questions.solutionHtml:
but rather with hypoplastic or amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura [ITP]: ITP is characterized by autoimmune destruction of platelets. It typically presents with isolated thrombocytopenia and may show an increased number of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow due to compensatory production.

 

Option B. Systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE]: SLE can cause thrombocytopenia due to autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction. Megakaryocytes may be increased in the bone marrow as the body tries to compensate for the peripheral platelet destruction.

 

Option D. Disseminated intravascular coagulation [DIC]: DIC is a condition that leads to the systemic activation of the coagulation cascade, resulting in widespread microthrombi and secondary consumption of platelets and coagulation factors. This can also lead to a compensatory increase in megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In megakaryocytic thrombocytopenia, there is an increase in bone marrow megakaryocytes as a compensatory mechanism for peripheral platelet destruction, but in aplastic anemia, there is bone marrow failure and reduced megakaryocytes.

Option A. Platelet function tests assess platelet aggregation and adhesion, which are not measured by the aPTT. The aPTT test measures factors in the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways but not platelet function.

The activated Partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) test evaluates the factors of the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways and is used to monitor heparin therapy, diagnose coagulation factor deficiencies, and assess the potential presence of inhibitors.

Explanation:

 

Option A. Factor X deficiency: Factor X deficiency is a rare bleeding disorder where the clotting factor X is either deficient or not functioning properly. It typically presents with a prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), which are not normal in this case.

 

Option C. von Willebrand disease: Von Willebrand disease is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder and is caused by a qualitative or quantitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor (vWF). vWF is crucial for platelet adhesion; however, PT and aPTT can be normal in mild cases, but there's often an abnormal bleeding time or abnormal vWF assays.

 

Option D. Bernard-Soulier disease: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is another rare platelet disorder, caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex, important for platelet adhesion to the vascular subendothelium. Similar to Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia, PT and aPTT are normal, but the platelet function is impaired, leading to bleeding.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of normal PT and aPTT despite bleeding symptoms points towards a platelet function disorder rather than a clotting factor deficiency. Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia and Bernard-Soulier syndrome are both characterized by normal coagulation tests and abnormal platelet function; however, Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia is generally considered more likely when these two conditions are indistinguishable based on clinical and laboratory findings.

questions.stem: A 25 years old asymptomatic pregnant female underwent a pre-op coagulation test. Her bleeding time is 3 minutes, PT is 15/14sec, a PTT is 45/35 sec, platelet count is 2.5 lac/ mm3 and factor VIII levels were 60IU/dL. What is her most likely diagnosis?

ext-align:justify;"> 

(3 minutes is the normal bleeding time)

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Factor IX deficiency: Factor IX deficiency, also known as Hemophilia B or Christmas disease, is a bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency of clotting factor IX. It is an X-linked recessive disorder, making it much less likely in females. It presents with a prolonged aPTT but normal PT and bleeding time, which does not fully match the patient's profile since her PT and bleeding time are within normal limits.

 

Option B. Lupus anticoagulant: The presence of lupus anticoagulant, an autoimmune inhibitor, is associated with prolonged aPTT and may also lead to a prolonged PT. It is part of the antiphospholipid syndrome and can cause both bleeding and thrombotic episodes. Patients often have thrombocytopenia, which is not the case here as the patient has a normal platelet count.

 

Option D. VWD – Type III: Von Willebrand Disease (VWD) Type III is the most severe form of VWD and is characterized by a markedly reduced or absent von Willebrand factor, leading to a significant bleeding tendency. Patients usually have a prolonged bleeding time and a decreased factor VIII activity, which is not consistent with this patient's normal bleeding time and near-normal factor VIII levels.

 

Educational Objective:

 

This patient’s normal bleeding time and PT but prolonged aPTT, along with the presence of normal factor VIII activity, suggest the presence of an inhibitor against factor VIII rather than a deficiency, which is consistent with acquired hemophilia.

questions.stem: True about prothrombin time to:

options.label: A
options.text: Immediate refrigeration to preserve factor viability

questions.solutionHtml:
and VIII, which can deteriorate over time at room temperature.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Immediate refrigeration to preserve factor viability: While it's true that certain coagulation factors are temperature sensitive, prothrombin time (PT) testing typically requires the sample to be kept at room temperature to prevent the cold activation of factors and potential precipitation of fibrinogen. Immediate refrigeration is not required for PT.

 

Option B. Platelet-rich plasma is essential: PT is actually performed on platelet-poor plasma, not platelet-rich plasma. The presence of platelets can affect the test results by providing phospholipid surfaces that could artificially shorten the clotting time.

 

Option D. Activated with kaolin: PT is not activated with kaolin. Instead, thromboplastin (a combination of tissue factor and phospholipids) is used to activate the extrinsic pathway of coagulation. Kaolin is used as an activator in the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) test, which evaluates the intrinsic pathway.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The PT test must be done on platelet-poor plasma and usually within 2 hours of sample collection to ensure accurate results, using thromboplastin for activation.

options.text: Decreased platelet count and increased bleeding time

questions.answerText: Normal platelet count and increased bleeding time
questions.solutionHtml:
,serif">Option A. Normal platelet count and normal bleeding time: This option would suggest no defect in platelet function or number, which would not typically be associated with a bleeding disorder.

 

Option C. Decreased platelet count and increased bleeding time: This suggests a quantitative defect of platelets, such as thrombocytopenia, rather than a functional defect. Although patients with thrombocytopenia will also have an increased bleeding time, the platelet count in functional defects remains normal.

 

Option D. Normal platelet count and decreased bleeding time: A decreased bleeding time indicates an efficient clotting process, which would not align with platelet function defects.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Platelet function defects present with a normal platelet count but impaired function, leading to an increased bleeding time, whereas quantitative disorders would show an altered platelet count.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with no significant past medical history is brought to the pediatrician by his parents who are concerned about his recent onset of spontaneous bruising and a single episode of nose bleeding that took longer than expected to cease. The child has no known allergies, and there is no family history of bleeding disorders. On physical examination, the paediatrician notes several bruises of varying sizes on his legs and arms, as well as petechiae on his ankles. Initial laboratory tests reveal an elevated prothrombin time (PT) and an elevated activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), but a normal platelet count and bleeding time (BT). What is the most likely defect in this child's coagulation pathway?
questions.solutionHtml:
n",serif">Explanation:

 

Option A. Extrinsic pathway: A defect in the extrinsic pathway would typically lead to an isolated elevation of PT, as this pathway is evaluated by the PT test. This does not explain the elevated aPTT observed in the patient.

 

Option B. Intrinsic pathway: A defect in the intrinsic pathway would typically result in an isolated elevation of aPTT, as this pathway is evaluated by the aPTT test. This also does not explain the elevated PT observed in the patient.

 

Option C. Platelet function: Platelet function defects usually result in a prolonged bleeding time (BT) and normal coagulation tests (PT and aPTT). Since the patient has a normal BT, this is unlikely to be the correct diagnosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Defect in the extrinsic pathway causes elevation of PT
  • Defect in the intrinsic pathway causes elevation of aPTT.
  • Defect in common pathway cause elevation of both PT and aPTT.
  • Platelet function defect causes elevation of BT.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old female presents with easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after minor injuries. She has a family history of bleeding disorders. Which of the following is caused by VWF factor deficiency?
questions.solutionHtml:
pan style="font-size:12pt;">Von Willebrand factor (VWF) deficiency can lead to several effects on the coagulation process:

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Defect platelet function: True. VWF plays a crucial role in platelet adhesion by binding to platelets and stabilizing the interaction between platelets and the damaged blood vessel wall. Its reduced levels lead to reduced platelet functioning.

 

Option B. Reduced factor VIII in plasma: True. VWF serves as a carrier protein for factor VIII, protecting it from rapid clearance and degradation. Therefore, a deficiency in VWF can result in decreased levels of factor VIII in the plasma.

 

Option C. Defective platelet adhesion: True. VWF is essential for the initial adhesion of platelets to the damaged blood vessel wall, facilitating the formation of a stable plug at the site of injury.

 

So, the correct answer is (d) All of the above. Von Willebrand factor deficiency affects both platelet function and factor VIII levels in the plasma.

 

Educational objective:

 

VWF deficiency impairs platelet adhesion and aggregation at the site of vascular injury, and reduces the plasma level of factor VIII by decreasing its stability in circulation.

questions.stem: Irradiation of blood prior to transfusion prevents which of the following complications?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A: (TRALI - Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury): TRALI is a serious complication characterized by acute respiratory distress following transfusion. It is thought to be caused by donor antibodies against recipient leukocytes. Irradiation does not prevent TRALI.

 

Option B: (HLA alloimmunization): HLA alloimmunization can occur when a patient develops antibodies against HLA antigens from transfused blood. While leukoreduction can reduce the risk, irradiation of blood products does not prevent HLA alloimmunization.

 

Option D: (Immunomodulation): Immunomodulation refers to the potential immune system changes in transfusion recipients, potentially leading to an increased risk of postoperative infections and malignancy recurrence. Irradiation’s role in preventing immunomodulation is not clearly established.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Irradiation of white and red blood cells prior to transfusion is primarily used to prevent graft versus host disease.

  • Donor T cells attack recipient tissues.
  • Occurs particularly in immunocompromised patients (e.g., post-transplant, chemotherapy).
  • It is often fatal.
  • Irradiation (typically with 25–30 Gy gamma rays) prevents T-cell proliferation.

rong> blood transfusions.

Option A. Malaria is routinely screened for in donated blood because it is caused by parasites transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. Screening helps prevent the transmission of malaria through blood transfusions.

Option B.  Hepatitis B is a viral infection that can be transmitted through blood transfusions. Screening for Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is essential to prevent the transmission of the virus to recipients of donated blood.
